newsitem.title: USA: UPS, Teamsters dig in for an extended battle.
newsitem.headline: UPS, Teamsters dig in for an extended battle.

text.p: United Parcel Service and the Teamsters began digging in for a prolonged strike on Sunday after three days of talks with a federal mediator failed to end the biggest U.S. labour dispute in a quarter century.

As the walkout by 185,000 union members entered its seventh day, the world's leading parcel delivery company warned that Teamster demands for pay, pension benefits and full-time work threatened to jeopardise its competitive edge against non-unionized rivals in the package shipping industry.
"The demands of the union would have made it impossible for UPS to serve its customers and remain competitive," the company said in a statement.
Labour Secretary Alexis Herman said she would call the heads of UPS and the Teamsters to try to end the weeklong walkout.
"I plan to do that today," Herman said on the NBC television programme "Meet the Press."
"I want to find out what it's going to take from them to get these talks moving in the right direction," she said.
Atlanta-based UPS normally handles 80 percent of deliveries to businesses, manufacturers, hospitals and consumers in the United States, with daily volumes nearing 12 million parcels.

But the strike has reduced the giant company to less than 10 percent of its usual volume, provoking warnings from national business leaders of a threat to economic growth and a potential for layoffs among small- and mid-size firms.
A privately held company with annual revenues of $22.4 billion, UPS said it had already lost hundreds of millions of dollars as a result of the strike.

The latest talks, which started on Thursday, broke off on Saturday after just two hours of bargaining and with the two sides no closer to a settlement than they were when the walkout started last Monday. An earlier round of negotiations lasted 17 hours before collapsing late last Sunday night.

UPS has refused to budge from a demand that the Teamsters union allow members to vote on a management proposal that the company describes as its "last, best and final offer." Union leaders rejected the package more than a week ago.
But over the weekend, company executives blamed the strike on union intransigence.

"The position of the Teamsters continues to be unrealistic," UPS Chief Executive James Kelly told reporters outside the offices of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service in Washington, where Saturday's talks were held.

The Teamsters have criticised the company for refusing to end sub-contracting and create thousands of new full-time jobs each year from part-time jobs, which account for 60 percent of the company's 301,000 domestic workers.
UPS said the real issue was the Teamsters' refusal to let the company withdraw from a union-administered multi-employer pension plan that includes a host of other companies, mostly trucking firms.

The latest breakdown in negotiations raised the possibility that UPS would resort to using replacement workers to supplement a depleted work force of 50,000 non-union employees who have been shifted to field operations.
"We're heading back to Atlanta to make some difficult decisions we have to make going forward," Kelly said.
But the Teamsters showed no sign of losing their conviction.
"They said they're going back to Atlanta, and we're on our way back to the picket lines," Teamsters President Ron Carey said after talks ended.
"It's vital to the interests of our members, their families and to the interests of working people in this country. Part-time America won't work."
Striking UPS employees also said they were ready to see the fight through to the end.

"We're encouraging our people to stay out here, and stay strong, and stay united. As far as we're concerned, that's all we can do at the present moment," UPS striker David Gamblin said while on picket-line duty in Atlanta.
Federal mediator John Calhoun Wells, who conducted the latest round of talks, said he would reconvene negotiations when the time was right. But he did not say when that might be.
